q: Acetone is deprotonated at an α-carbon. Which structure is the major resonance contributor of the resulting anion?
h: Draw both resonance forms of the anion. Which atom is better at carrying a negative charge?
w: The enolate has two resonance forms: one with the charge on the α-carbon and one with the charge on oxygen and a C=C bond. Both have full octets, so the better contributor is the one with the negative charge on the more electronegative atom, oxygen. That oxyanion form is the major contributor, which is why the α-H of a ketone (pKa ≈ 19–20) is far more acidic than an alkane C–H.
x: This carbanion form is a real resonance contributor of the enolate, but a minor one: carbon is less able than oxygen to carry the negative charge.
This neutral enol is a tautomer of acetone (a different compound with an O–H bond), not a resonance form of the anion.
This is the isopropoxide ion, the conjugate base of 2-propanol; forming it would need a hydride added to the carbonyl, not removal of an α-proton.

q: Acetic acid (pK<sub>a</sub> 4.8) is about 10<sup>11</sup> times more acidic than ethanol (pK<sub>a</sub> 16). What is the main reason?
c: In acetate the negative charge is delocalized by resonance over two oxygen atoms.
The methyl group of acetic acid donates electrons and weakens the O–H bond.
The acidic oxygen of acetic acid is sp-hybridized, so it holds the charge closer to the nucleus.
Inductive withdrawal by the carbonyl group alone; resonance plays no part in acetate.
h: Both acids lose a proton from oxygen. Compare how the negative charge is distributed in acetate and in ethoxide.
w: In both conjugate bases the charge starts on oxygen (same atom), so the difference comes from resonance: acetate spreads its charge equally over two oxygens (both C–O bonds are the same length), whereas ethoxide holds it on one oxygen. The carbonyl group's inductive withdrawal adds a smaller contribution.
x: Alkyl groups are weakly electron-donating, which would destabilize the anion and make the acid weaker, not stronger; ethanol has an alkyl group too.
The OH oxygen of acetic acid is not sp-hybridized; in acetate both oxygens share the charge through a conjugated system. Orbital (hybridization) arguments apply to C–H acids such as alkynes.
Induction contributes, but the main factor is resonance; the two C–O bonds of acetate are identical in length, which shows the charge is shared.

q: Rank compounds I–IV from most basic to least basic (as Brønsted bases in water).
h: A nitrogen lone pair is most basic when localized. Is each lone pair delocalized into a ring or a C=O group? Is an alkyl group donating to it?
w: Basicity follows the pKa of each conjugate acid. Ethylamine (II, pKaH ≈ 10.7): localized sp3 lone pair with an electron-donating alkyl group. Ammonia (IV, ≈ 9.2): localized but no alkyl group. Aniline (III, ≈ 4.6): the lone pair is delocalized into the benzene ring. Acetamide (I, ≈ −0.5): the lone pair is strongly delocalized onto the carbonyl oxygen, so the amide is barely basic. Order: II > IV > III > I.
x: In water, ethylamine (pK<sub>a</sub>H 10.7) is more basic than ammonia (9.2) because the ethyl group donates electron density and stabilizes the ammonium ion.
Amide nitrogen lone pairs are delocalized onto a C=O oxygen, which is far more effective than delocalization into a benzene ring; acetamide is much less basic than aniline.
Aniline's aromatic ring does not make it a strong base; delocalizing the lone pair into the ring lowers its basicity by about a million-fold compared with alkylamines.

q: When this compound is treated with one equivalent of HCl, which labeled atom is protonated?
h: Compare a localized amine lone pair with the lone pairs of an amide (both N and O) and an ether oxygen. Which conjugate acid has the highest pK<sub>a</sub>?
w: The tertiary amine nitrogen c has a localized sp3 lone pair; its conjugate acid has pKa ≈ 10. An amide is protonated (when at all) on its carbonyl oxygen d (pKaH ≈ −0.5); the amide nitrogen b is even less basic because its lone pair is delocalized into the C=O. The ether oxygen a has pKaH ≈ −3.5. So atom c, the amine, is protonated.
x: The amide N–H nitrogen looks like an amine, but its lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl; it is the least basic site of an amide.
The amide oxygen is the more basic site within the amide, but its conjugate acid has pK<sub>a</sub> near −0.5, about 10<sup>10</sup> times more acidic than a protonated amine.
Ether oxygens are very weak bases (pK<sub>a</sub>H ≈ −3.5); an amine in the same molecule is protonated first.

q: Use the table to find K<sub>eq</sub> for: CF<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>O<sup>−</sup> ⇌ CF<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>O<sup>−</sup> + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH
h: Identify the acid on each side. K<sub>eq</sub> = 10<sup>(pK<sub>a</sub> of the product acid − pK<sub>a</sub> of the reactant acid)</sup>.
w: The reactant acid is 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol (12.4); the product acid is ethanol (16.0). Keq = 10(16.0 − 12.4) = 103.6 ≈ 4 × 103, products favored. The three fluorines stabilize the alkoxide inductively, so ethoxide deprotonates trifluoroethanol.
x: This uses the exponent with the wrong sign. The stronger acid (CF<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) is on the left, so K<sub>eq</sub> > 1.
This divides the pK<sub>a</sub> values (16.0/12.4). Since pK<sub>a</sub> is a logarithm, K<sub>eq</sub> = 10 raised to the difference.
This adds the pK<sub>a</sub> values. K<sub>eq</sub> depends only on their difference, 3.6 units.

q: At equal concentrations in water, HCl (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ −7) and HBr (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ −9) give solutions with the same pH. Why?
c: Both transfer their protons essentially completely to water, so H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> is the strongest acid present in each.
Chloride and bromide are both stabilized by hydrogen bonding to the same extent, which cancels the difference.
Water is a stronger acid than both HCl and HBr, so neither ionizes significantly.
The pK<sub>a</sub> values are too close to give any measurable difference in K<sub>eq</sub>.
h: What is the strongest acid that can exist in significant amounts in water? (pK<sub>a</sub> of H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> ≈ −1.7)
w: Any acid much stronger than H3O+ (pKa −1.7) protonates water completely, giving H3O+ + X−. Water levels the strong acids: H3O+ is the strongest acid present in each solution, so their difference only shows up in a less basic solvent (such as acetic acid).
x: Solvation of the anions does not cancel out; the true reason is that both acids ionize completely, so only H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> remains as the acid.
This reverses the acidities. HCl and HBr are far stronger acids than water (15.7) or H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> (−1.7), so they ionize completely.
Two pK<sub>a</sub> units is a 100-fold difference in K<sub>a</sub>, which would be measurable; it disappears in water only because both ionize completely.

q: Which base/solvent combination converts 1-hexyne (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25) essentially completely to its acetylide ion?
h: Two conditions: the base's conjugate acid must be weaker than the alkyne, and the solvent must not be a stronger acid than the alkyne.
w: NH2− (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 38) deprotonates the alkyne with Keq ≈ 1013, and the solvent NH3 is a weaker acid than the alkyne, so it cannot reprotonate the acetylide. NaNH2 in liquid NH3 works.
x: Hydroxide is too weak a base (water pK<sub>a</sub> 15.7), and water as solvent would reprotonate any acetylide formed.
Ethoxide is too weak (ethanol pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16), and ethanol solvent is about 10<sup>9</sup> times more acidic than the alkyne.
Butyllithium is a strong enough base, but methanol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 15.5) is a far stronger acid than the alkyne; BuLi is destroyed by the solvent, giving butane and lithium methoxide.

q: Which structure is the conjugate acid of acetone?
h: A conjugate acid has one more H<sup>+</sup> (one more proton and one more positive charge) than the base.
w: Adding H+ to a lone pair of the carbonyl oxygen gives protonated acetone, (CH3)2C=OH+ (pKa ≈ −7). Its formula is acetone + H+.
x: This is the enolate, the conjugate base of acetone (one H+ removed).
This is the enol, a tautomer of acetone with the same formula; nothing was added.
This is 2-propanol, which has two more hydrogens than acetone and no charge; it is a reduction product, not a conjugate acid.

q: Using the table, which base converts acetone (pKa 19.2) almost completely to its enolate?
h: For each base, compare the pK<sub>a</sub> of its conjugate acid with 19.2. K<sub>eq</sub> must be much larger than 1.
w: Keq = 10(pKa of conjugate acid − 19.2). For LDA: 10(36 − 19.2) ≈ 1017, essentially complete. tert-Butoxide: 10−1.2 ≈ 0.06; ethoxide: 10−3.2; hydroxide: 10−3.5. Those alkoxide and hydroxide bases form only small equilibrium amounts of enolate.
x: tert-Butoxide is a strong, bulky base, but tert-butanol (18) is a slightly stronger acid than acetone (19.2), so Keq ≈ 0.06; most acetone stays protonated.
Ethanol (16.0) is more acidic than acetone, so ethoxide gives K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>−3</sup>; only a small fraction of enolate forms.
Water (15.7) is more acidic than acetone, so hydroxide gives K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>−3.5</sup>; it makes only traces of enolate.

q: Fluorine is more electronegative than iodine, yet HI (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ −10) is a far stronger acid than HF (pK<sub>a</sub> 3.2). Which explanation is best?
c: Iodide is much larger, so its charge is spread over more volume, and the H–I bond is weaker.
Iodine is more electronegative than fluorine in water, because of hydrogen bonding to the solvent.
Fluoride is stabilized by resonance, which makes HF less likely to ionize in water.
HI has an sp-hybridized iodine, while HF has an sp<sup>3</sup>-hybridized fluorine.
h: Within a row of the periodic table electronegativity controls acidity. What factor dominates down a column?
w: Down a group, atom size dominates: I− spreads its charge over a much larger, more polarizable volume than F−, and the long H–I bond is weak. Both factors favor ionization of HI. Electronegativity is the deciding factor only across a row (C < N < O < F).
x: Iodine is less electronegative than fluorine in any medium; electronegativity would actually predict HF to be the stronger acid.
Fluoride has no resonance; it is a single atom. Its small size concentrates the charge, which makes F<sup>−</sup> less stable, not more.
Hybridization arguments compare acids with the same atom (such as sp vs sp<sup>3</sup> C–H). It is not the reason for the HF/HI difference.

q: Rank the labeled hydrogens from most acidic to least acidic.
h: All three are C–H bonds with no resonance stabilization of the anion. What is different is the hybridization of each carbon.
w: With the atom the same and no resonance, the orbital holding the lone pair decides. The anion from a (sp, 50% s) is most stable (pKa ≈ 25), then b (sp2, 33% s, ≈ 44), then c (sp3, 25% s, ≈ 50): a > b > c. Carbon c is neither allylic nor propargylic, so it gets no resonance help.
x: This reverses the trend. More s character holds the lone pair closer to the nucleus and stabilizes the carbanion, so the sp C–H is the most acidic.
A vinylic sp<sup>2</sup> C–H (≈ 44) is far less acidic than a terminal alkyne C–H (≈ 25).
The sp3 C–H on c has the least s character, so it is less acidic than the sp2 vinylic C–H on b.

q: In the phenoxide ion, resonance places the negative charge on oxygen and on which ring carbons?
c: The two ortho carbons and the para carbon
Only the ring carbon bonded to oxygen
h: Push the oxygen lone pair into the ring and move the π electrons one step at a time. Which carbons pick up the lone pair?
w: Each resonance step moves the negative charge two atoms along the ring, so from the oxygen it reaches the carbons at the ortho, para and other ortho positions. The meta carbons and the ipso carbon never carry the charge. This is why groups at ortho/para positions (such as NO2) affect phenol acidity most.
x: The meta carbons are skipped: charge alternates around the ring and never lands on them.
The charge is not spread over all six carbons; it alternates, reaching only ortho and para.
The ipso carbon forms a C=O double bond in the contributors that carry ring charge; it never holds the negative charge itself.

q: Which species is the strongest acid? (Use the hybridization of the atom that bears the proton's lone pair in each conjugate base.)
h: The strongest acid has the weakest conjugate base. Compare how tightly each neutral base holds its lone pair: what is the hybridization of the atom being protonated?
w: Remove the proton to get each conjugate base: CH3OH, CH3NH2, acetone and acetonitrile. The nitrile nitrogen's lone pair is in an sp orbital (50% s), held tightly, so acetonitrile is the weakest base and protonated acetonitrile (pKa ≈ −10) is the strongest acid. Protonated acetone (sp2 O, ≈ −7) and protonated methanol (sp3 O, ≈ −2.5) are weaker; methylammonium (≈ 10.6) is weakest.
x: Protonated acetone is a very strong acid (≈ −7), but the sp lone pair of a nitrile is held even more tightly than the sp<sup>2</sup> lone pair of a carbonyl oxygen.
Protonated methanol (≈ −2.5) is a strong acid, but its sp<sup>3</sup> oxygen lone pair is a better base than the sp nitrogen of a nitrile, so it gives up its proton less readily.
Methylammonium (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 10.6) is the weakest acid here because methylamine is a good base; a positive charge alone does not make a strong acid.

q: Ethylmagnesium bromide is added to ethanol. What are the main products?
c: No reaction; Grignard reagents are stable in alcohols
h: The C–Mg bond is highly polarized toward carbon, so the ethyl group behaves like a carbanion (conjugate acid pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 50). What does ethanol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16) offer it?
w: A Grignard reagent is an extremely strong base. Ethanol (pKa ≈ 16) is about 1034 times more acidic than ethane (≈ 50), so a fast proton transfer gives ethane and the magnesium alkoxide CH3CH2OMgBr. For this reason Grignard reagents must be prepared and used in dry, aprotic ethers.
x: Grignard reagents do not couple with alcohols to form new C–C bonds; proton transfer from the O–H is much faster.
An ether would require the alkyl group to attack oxygen and displace OH, which does not happen; the fast reaction is proton transfer.
Grignard reagents are destroyed by any O–H, N–H or S–H acid; that is why they are made in dry ether or THF.

q: Rank these species in order of increasing acidity: NH3, H2O, NH4+, H3O+
h: Recall the pK<sub>a</sub> values: NH<sub>3</sub> ≈ 38, H<sub>2</sub>O 15.7, NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> 9.2, H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> −1.7.
w: pKa values: NH3 ≈ 38, H2O 15.7, NH4+ 9.2, H3O+ −1.7. Order: NH3 < H2O < NH4+ < H3O+. Two trends combine: O–H is more acidic than N–H (electronegativity), and a positive charge on the acid makes it much more acidic than its neutral form.
x: Ammonium (9.2) is more acidic than water (15.7): the positive charge makes losing H<sup>+</sup> much easier.
Oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen, so water is more acidic than ammonia, and H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> is more acidic than NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>.
This puts the cations as the weakest acids. Positively charged acids lose a proton far more readily than their neutral counterparts.
